Partial differential equation (F(x,t,u,ut​,ux​,uxx​,…)=0)

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 56k Articles: 947
A partial differential equation relates an unknown function of several independent variables to its partial derivatives. For u(x,t), the notation ut​=∂u/∂t means changing time while holding position fixed; uxx​=∂2u/∂x2 measures how its spatial slope changes. Unlike an ordinary differential equation, a partial differential equation can describe an entire evolving profile rather than a single trajectory.
The heat equation ut​=Duxx​ smooths spatial variations, the transport equation ut​+cux​=0 moves them, and Laplace's equation Δu=0 describes a spatial equilibrium. Here D>0 is a diffusivity, c is a velocity, and Δ is the Laplacian. The periodic heat and transport comparison makes the difference visible using identical initial conditions.
A partial differential equation usually supplies a local rule rather than a complete answer. For example, every u(x,t)=A+Bx satisfies the heat equation with zero PDE source term; data select which profile is relevant. A complete problem specifies its domain of a function, coefficients, initial conditions, boundary conditions, and meaning of solution of a partial differential equation. A well-posed problem has existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence on initial data in stated spaces; the equation alone guarantees none of these.[ref]

Initial and boundary data for evolution equations

Words: 217 Articles: 1
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
On 0<x<L, t>0, an initial condition u(x,0)=g(x) gives the starting profile. For the heat equation, Dirichlet boundary conditions u(0,t)=a(t), u(L,t)=b(t) can model ends held at prescribed temperatures. Alternatively, zero Neumann boundary conditions describe insulated ends in the constant-conductivity model. These choices can produce different evolutions from the same initial condition.
For a continuous classical solution reaching the corners, the Dirichlet boundary data must satisfy g(0)=a(0) and g(L)=b(0); higher smoothness can require further compatibility. In dimensionless variables, a complete worked heat equation problem is
ut​=uxx​,0<x<1,t>0,u(x,0)=x+sin(πx),u(0,t)=0,u(1,t)=1.
(1)
Its exact classical solution is u(x,t)=x+e−π2tsin(πx). The straight profile x is the equilibrium; the extra bump decays. Substituting verifies the equation and every datum, and the energy estimate proves uniqueness among smooth solutions with these data.
For the transport equation with c>0 on the same interval, prescribe an inflow transport boundary condition only at x=0. Backtracking a characteristic curve gives g(x−ct) if x≥ct, and a(t−x/c) otherwise. Values at x=L are determined by this formula; independently prescribing them can make the problem inconsistent.[ref]

Source term in a partial differential equation (f(x,t))

Words: 42
Initial and boundary data for evolution equations OurBigBook.com
A prescribed PDE source term changes the heat equation to ut​=Duxx​+f(x,t), or the transport equation to ut​+cux​=f(x,t). If u is a temperature, f has units of temperature per time. The formulas below assume f=0; a nonzero PDE source term can change the spatial average even with periodic boundary conditions.

Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation (ut​+uux​+uxx​+uxxxx​=0)

Words: 140 Articles: 1
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation ut​+uux​+uxx​+uxxxx​=0 combines destabilizing long-wave growth, stabilizing fourth-order diffusion, and nonlinear transport. Its potential form is Φt​=−Φxx​−Φxxxx​+(Φx​)2, with u=−2Φx​. It arises as a long-wave phase amplitude equation near loss of the Benjamin-Feir stability condition. On a domain of period P, the zero solution's Fourier modes grow at rate k2−k4, k=2πn/P.

Primary periodic bifurcation of the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation

Words: 88

Burgers' equation (ut​+uux​=νuxx​)

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
Burgers' equation is the one-dimensional partial differential equation
ut​+uux​=νuxx​,ν≥0.
(3)
The term uux​ supplies nonlinear transport in a transport equation: the transported value u is also its own characteristic speed when ν=0. Larger values catch up with smaller values ahead of them, steepening a decreasing profile. The diffusion term νuxx​ opposes this steepening. Positive ν gives the viscous Burgers equation; setting ν=0 gives the Inviscid Burgers equation.
This small equation makes three different behaviors accessible in one model: Burgers characteristic breaking from continuous decreasing data, an entropy shock for a downward step, and a rarefaction wave for an upward step. The Burgers Riemann problem with positive flux and the Viscous Burgers travelling shock below give exact examples. These are mathematical calculations with chosen data; the figures contain no experimental measurements.
Unless stated otherwise, take x∈R, t≥0, constant ν, no PDE source term, and an initial condition u(x,0)=u0​(x). There are no finite endpoints requiring boundary conditions. Where a profile has different limiting states at x=±∞, those states are specified explicitly. On a finite interval, boundary conditions become part of the problem: positive diffusion normally requires a condition at each endpoint, whereas the Inviscid Burgers equation requires appropriate inflow transport boundary conditions. With dimensional variables, u has units of velocity and ν of kinematic viscosity; all numerical examples below use dimensionless quantities.

Viscous Burgers equation (ut​+uux​=νuxx​)

Words: 1k Articles: 14
Burgers' equation OurBigBook.com
The viscous Burgers equation combines a nonlinear transport equation with diffusion with constant ν>0. On the infinite line, a bounded initial condition gives a smooth function solving the equation for every positive time; a jump in the initial condition is smoothed rather than retained as a discontinuity. Small ν can nevertheless produce a steep layer, as the Viscous Burgers travelling shock illustrates. The Cole-Hopf transformation u=−2ν∂x​logϕ, with positive ϕ, converts this equation to the heat equation ϕt​=νϕxx​.[ref]
Positive diffusion also explains the admissibility of the inviscid limit. For the entropy flux for a scalar conservation law associated with η(u)=u2/2, direct multiplication by u gives
∂t​2u2​+∂x​3u3​=ν∂xx​2u2​−νux2​.
(4)
The last term is nonpositive. With convergence sufficient to pass to the limit, the vanishing viscosity approximation therefore retains an entropy inequality rather than just the weak solution equation. For general bounded data, the full Kruzhkov entropy inequalities specify the entropy solution; the quadratic identity is a useful illustration of dissipation.[ref]

Choosing the center U(0)=s gives the displayed hyperbolic tangent profile. Its characteristic width scales as ν/(uL​−uR​); a smaller positive ν makes a thinner smooth layer.

Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
The domain of dependence of a solution value consists of the initial and boundary locations whose data can influence it. For ut​+aux​=0 on the whole line, u(x,t)=u(x−at,0), so its initial-data domain of dependence is the foot of the characteristic. For a finite-difference scheme, repeated stencil dependencies determine a numerical domain of dependence. The Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy condition requires the numerical domain to cover the physical one for convergence; it is necessary under its usual hyperbolic hypotheses, but not in general sufficient for stability.

Linear partial differential equation

Partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A linear partial differential equation is a partial differential equation in which the unknown function and its partial derivatives occur linearly, with coefficients independent of the unknown. Its homogeneous solutions obey the superposition principle.
For example, the heat equation permits adding independently decaying Fourier modes. For an equation Lu=f with a fixed nonzero PDE source term, adding two solutions gives L(u+v)=2f, so the sum generally solves a different problem. Likewise, adding solutions adds their initial conditions and boundary conditions.

Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem OurBigBook.com
For a linear differential operator with real analytic coefficients, a classical solution with zero Cauchy data on a real analytic non-characteristic hypersurface vanishes locally near that hypersurface. The solution itself need not be real analytic. A proof solves the real analytic inhomogeneous formal adjoint problem against polynomial sources, annihilates all polynomial moments using boundary jets, and uses polynomial density to force the solution to vanish.
Parabolic-cap proof of Holmgren uniqueness
Words: 74
Holmgren uniqueness theorem OurBigBook.com
Near a non-characteristic plane x=0, use the small cap ωε​={x>0, x+y2<ε}. Its curved face is non-characteristic by continuity of the principal symbol. A polynomial coordinate change flattens that face. Uniform real analytic coefficient bounds and the uniform Cauchy radius for polynomial forcing solve P∗v=g throughout a common cap, with zero boundary jet on the curved face. The complete boundary-jet condition for formal adjoints then gives ∫ωε​​ug=0 for every polynomial g. Uniform approximation of uˉ gives ∫∣u∣2=0. Repeating on the other side of the plane proves two-sided local uniqueness.

Uniform Cauchy radius for polynomial forcing

Words: 89
Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem OurBigBook.com
For a linear real analytic non-characteristic Cauchy problem for a partial differential equation with zero data, the local real analytic radius may be chosen uniformly over polynomial forcing terms. Fix an analyticity exponent R−1. Each polynomial, including a polynomial obtained by a polynomial coordinate change, satisfies the corresponding factorial derivative bound with some finite prefactor, uniformly over a compact parameter range. Divide the forcing by that prefactor to put all such data in one fixed majorant class. The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem supplies a common radius, and linearity rescales the solution back without shrinking it. This argument does not bound the amplitudes of the resulting solutions uniformly.

General-order Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem

Words: 73
Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem OurBigBook.com
A real analytic system solved for the highest normal derivatives, with real analytic Cauchy data, has a unique local real analytic solution. For common order m, its normal form is ∂tm​U=F(t,x,{∂tj​∂xα​U:j<m, j+∣α∣≤m}). An invertible coefficient/Jacobian matrix for the highest normal derivatives is the system's non-characteristic hypersurface condition. A real analytic coordinate change flattens the initial hypersurface, and adjoining derivatives through order m−1 reduces the problem to a first-order real analytic system. Uniqueness here is in the real analytic class; it does not assert Hadamard well-posedness in smooth or Sobolev norms.

Classical solution

Words: 224 Articles: 2
Solution of a partial differential equation OurBigBook.com
A classical solution has enough ordinary derivatives for the differential equation and its data to hold pointwise. For the heat equation, ut​ and uxx​ should be continuous in the interior, with the specified initial and boundary traces. A weak solution instead imposes an integrated identity, allowing less regular data; uniqueness must always be stated for the solution class used.

Positive-time smoothing for a semilinear heat equation

Words: 89
Classical solution OurBigBook.com
For a semilinear partial differential equation ut​=Δu+F(u) with smooth F and smooth fixed boundary data, local boundedness permits positive-time elliptic regularity and parabolic smoothing. If ut​ is continuous with values in a Hölder space, elliptic estimates first give continuous C2,β spatial regularity for u. Time difference quotients then solve a linear parabolic equation with coefficient converging to F′(u); smoothing away from the initial time gives ut​∈C(C2), hence u∈C1(C2). It is essential to gain spatial regularity for the time derivative too; u∈C(C2)∩C1(C0) alone does not imply C1(C2).

Classical solution OurBigBook.com
The notation Cb1,2​([0,∞)×R) ordinarily denotes functions with continuous time derivative and two continuous space derivatives, with the function and indicated derivatives bounded globally. A different condition, often intended in finite-horizon partial differential equations, is membership in Cb1,2​([0,T]×R) for each finite T, allowing bounds to grow with T. These conventions must be distinguished in a long-time growth problem: the second permits divergence with time; the first does not. There is no universal notation for the finite-horizon condition, so it should be stated explicitly.

A weak solution satisfies an integrated identity in which derivatives are transferred to test functions. It can therefore exist with fewer classical derivatives.

Weak solution OurBigBook.com

A viscosity supersolution satisfies the reverse inequality for tests touching from below. A viscosity solution satisfies both conditions. For F=−trD2u, these conditions are respectively Δϕ≥0 and Δϕ≤0. They make sense even when u has no classical second derivatives.
Continuous viscosity harmonic functions are classical (Δu=0)
Words: 105
Viscosity solution OurBigBook.com
Let a continuous function satisfy both viscosity inequalities for the Laplace operator. On any relatively compact ball, take its harmonic replacement h with matching boundary values. If u−h has a positive maximum, the function h+ε(R2−∣x−a∣2) still lies below u somewhere for sufficiently small positive ε, while matching it on the boundary. At an interior maximum of their difference it is a valid upper test, but its Laplacian is −2nε<0, a contradiction. The opposite perturbation excludes a negative minimum. Thus u=h throughout the ball and is a smooth harmonic function. A locally defined test is extended near its touching point using a smooth cutoff function when global tests are required.

A weak-strong uniqueness principle says that a weak solution with the same data as a sufficiently regular classical solution agrees with that solution throughout its interval of regular existence, within the specified weak class. The conclusion is class-dependent: all bounded weak solutions of a prescribed C1 linear transport field satisfy it, while nonlinear conservation laws require an admissibility condition such as an entropy solution condition.

Spherical harmonic matching with a derivative jump (Φnin​=an​rnPn​,Φnout​=an​r−n−1Pn​)

Words: 58
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
For a regular interior and a decaying exterior harmonic potential with continuous values on the unit sphere, the same coefficient multiplies the two radial branches of each Legendre polynomial mode. Its exterior-minus-interior radial derivative is −(2n+1)an​Pn​. Thus an axisymmetric prescribed jump jn​Pn​(cosθ) produces coefficient an​=−jn​/(2n+1). This diagonal matching rule reduces a spherical interface problem to its angular-mode coefficients.

Fourier solution of the strip Dirichlet problem (u(s,y)=g​(s)sinh(s(1−y))/sinhs)

Words: 87
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
For the Laplace equation on 0<y<1, prescribe bottom data g and zero top data. A horizontal Fourier transform reduces the equation to uyy​−s2u=0, giving the displayed multiplier and its limit 1−y at s=0. Integrable transformed data give a bounded inverse-transform solution. The bounded solution is unique by the maximum principle for harmonic functions, using barriers εcosh(δx)cos(δ(y−1/2)) for 0<δ<π on expanding rectangles. Without a growth condition, one can add eπxsin(πy), so the two boundary traces alone do not determine an arbitrary harmonic function on an infinite strip.

Harmonic matching across a circle with a derivative jump (Kn​=−jn​/(2n))

Words: 69
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
For a single-valued harmonic function tending to zero both at the origin and at infinity, match an angular Fourier series across the unit circle. A nonzero mode with continuous interface value Kn​cos(nθ) has interior field Kn​rncos(nθ) and exterior field Kn​r−ncos(nθ). Its exterior-minus-interior radial derivative is −2nKn​cos(nθ). Thus a prescribed jump coefficient jn​ determines Kn​=−jn​/(2n). Sine modes obey the same relation. The constant mode must have zero jump under these decay conditions.

Zero-boundary harmonic function with pointwise vertical decay (v(x,y)=ex2−y2sin(2xy))

Words: 64
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
The imaginary part of the entire function ez2 is a harmonic function. On the upper half-plane it vanishes at y=0 and tends to zero as y→∞ for every fixed x, but is nonzero and grows rapidly in the horizontal direction. Adding it to a Poisson integral preserves those boundary and vertical-decay conditions. A boundedness or suitable transform-growth condition is therefore needed to make the half-plane Dirichlet problem unique.

Exterior harmonic potential with no flux through a sphere (U=v0​(r+r03​/(2r2))cosθ)

Words: 54
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
An axisymmetric harmonic potential outside a sphere of radius r0​, with far field v0​rcosθ and zero radial derivative on the sphere, is
U=v0​(r+r03​/(2r2))cosθ.
(63)
The regular spherical expansion in Legendre polynomials fixes all coefficients. A spatial constant remains arbitrary if only the far-field gradient is specified, and is fixed by prescribing the potential difference at infinity.

Green function of the Laplacian (G(x,x′))

Words: 133 Articles: 2
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
In three dimensions,
−∇24π∣x−x′∣1​=δ(3)(x−x′).
(64)
Consequently the decaying solution of −∇2u=f in free space is
u(x)=4π1​∫R3​∣x−x′∣f(x′)​d3x′.
(65)
This is the free-space Green function for the negative Laplace operator.
Point-source potential with one compact spatial dimension (G(r,0)=4πLrcoth(πr/L)​)
Words: 76
Green function of the Laplacian OurBigBook.com
For three noncompact spatial coordinates of radius r and a circle of circumference L, the positive Laplace Green function on the source slice is G(r,0)=∑n∈Z​[4π2(r2+n2L2)]−1=(4πLr)−1coth(πr/L). At r≪L this is 1/(4π2r2); at r≫L it is 1/(4πLr) with exponentially small corrections. The long-distance coefficient also follows by replacing the dense image sum with L−1∫−∞∞​dy/(r2+y2)=π/(Lr). Electric and gravitational potentials inherit this crossover after multiplying by their signed source couplings.
Fundamental solution of the Laplace equation (Φ)
Words: 33
Green function of the Laplacian OurBigBook.com
Up to normalization and sign convention, a fundamental solution of the Laplace equation is Φ(x)=∣x∣2−n for n≥3 and Φ(x)=log∣x∣ for n=2. It is harmonic away from the origin and satisfies ΔΦ=cn​δ0​ distributionally.

Laplace equation in polar coordinates

Words: 103 Articles: 1
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
In plane polar coordinates, Laplace's equation is
r1​∂r∂​(r∂r∂ϕ​)+r21​∂θ2∂2ϕ​=0.
(66)
Separation of variables gives radial powers rn,r−n for positive angular modes and 1,logr for the zero mode.
Harmonic extension in a circular sector (Φ(r,θ)=∑n≥1​bn​(r/R)nπ/γsin(nπθ/γ))
Words: 79
Laplace equation in polar coordinates OurBigBook.com
For 0<θ<γ and 0<r<R, a bounded harmonic function that vanishes on the straight edges and has outer boundary data φ has coefficients
bn​=γ2​∫0γ​φ(θ)sinγnπθ​dθ.
(67)
This follows by separation of variables and Fourier orthogonality. Negative radial powers are excluded by boundedness at the vertex. Reflection-symmetric data φ(θ)=φ(γ−θ) have only odd Fourier modes. Knowing the resulting solution on the bisector determines all these odd coefficients by its radial power series. Without reflection symmetry, the even angular modes vanish on the bisector and cannot be recovered from that restriction alone.

Laplace equation in cylindrical coordinates

Words: 86 Articles: 1
Laplace equation OurBigBook.com
In cylindrical coordinates (r,θ,z), Laplace's equation is
r1​∂r∂​(r∂r∂ϕ​)+r21​∂θ2∂2ϕ​+∂z2∂2ϕ​=0.
(68)
Side boundary data do not determine a bounded harmonic function in a half-cylinder (e−j0,1​zJ0​(j0,1​r))
Words: 73
Laplace equation in cylindrical coordinates OurBigBook.com
In the unit half-cylinder z≥0, specifying only the curved-side boundary values does not determine a bounded harmonic function. The displayed nonzero function, where j0,1​ is a positive zero of the Bessel function of the first kind J0​, is regular at the axis, bounded, harmonic, and zero on r=1. It may be added to any particular solution without changing the side data, and even decays at infinity. Boundary information at the base z=0 is still required for uniqueness.

Radial Laplacian

Laplace operator OurBigBook.com
For radial u(r) in n dimensions, Δu=u′′+(n−1)u′/r.

Radial reduction and growth at infinity (u′′+2u′/r−u=g⟺y′′−y=rg,y=ru)

Words: 78
Radial Laplacian OurBigBook.com
For r>0, the substitution y=ru removes the first derivative in the three-dimensional radial Laplacian, since u′′+2u′/r=y′′/r. Bounded u at zero implies y(0)=0. Bounded u at infinity means y=O(r); it does not require bounded y. For example, constant forcing g=1 has the bounded particular solution u=−1, whose reduced function is y=−r. A Dirichlet half-line Green function for d2 minus 1 can still represent this solution when its integral converges, but the resulting reduced function has the growth demanded by the forcing.

Axisymmetric harmonic function

Words: 218 Articles: 2
Laplacian in spherical coordinates OurBigBook.com
Axisymmetric harmonic functions separate into radial powers times Legendre polynomials.
Axisymmetric harmonic extension from a sphere (Ψin​=∑ℓ​fℓ​(r/a)ℓPℓ​,Ψout​=∑ℓ​fℓ​(a/r)ℓ+1Pℓ​)
Words: 208 Articles: 1
Axisymmetric harmonic function OurBigBook.com
For boundary data f(u) on the sphere r=a, with u=cosθ, define its Legendre polynomial coefficients by fℓ​=(2ℓ+1)∫−11​f(u)Pℓ​(u)du/2. Separation of variables in the Laplace equation gives radial factors rℓ and r−ℓ−1. Regularity at the origin selects the first for the interior Dirichlet problem; decay at infinity selects the second for the exterior problem. Matching each boundary coefficient gives the displayed series. For continuous boundary data the resulting harmonic functions attain those data, with convergence interpreted through their harmonic extension rather than requiring uniform convergence of the unweighted boundary series. The maximum principle for harmonic functions proves uniqueness in the bounded interior and decaying exterior classes.
Odd Legendre extension for an equatorial Dirichlet plane
Words: 115
Axisymmetric harmonic extension from a sphere OurBigBook.com
Suppose the exterior of a sphere also has zero Dirichlet boundary conditions on the part of its equatorial plane outside the sphere. The plane separates the upper and lower domains. Extend the sphere data of each hemisphere oddly across the equator, and apply the axisymmetric harmonic extension from a sphere separately to these two odd extensions. Only odd-degree Legendre polynomials occur, and every such polynomial vanishes at u=cosθ=0. Thus the resulting harmonic function vanishes on the plane. For upper data f(u) on 0≤u≤1, the exterior coefficients are (2ℓ+1)∫01​f(u)Pℓ​(u)du for odd ℓ. If f(0)=0, the plane and sphere data agree at their shared edge. The same construction with the lower data gives the lower solution; their normal derivatives need not match through a conducting sheet.

A Laplacian eigenfunction satisfies −Δu=λu together with specified boundary conditions.

Laplacian eigenvalue (−Δu=λu)

Words: 38
Laplacian eigenfunction OurBigBook.com
A scalar λ for which a nonzero Laplacian eigenfunction satisfies this equation, with specified boundary conditions or on a closed manifold, is an eigenvalue of the positive Laplacian. A Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalue imposes zero boundary values; other boundary conditions generally change the spectrum.

Laplacian eigenfunction OurBigBook.com
A Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunction vanishes on the boundary and satisfies −Δu=λu.
Dirichlet eigenfunction supremum estimate (∥u∥∞​≤C(n)λn/4∥u∥2​)
Words: 58
Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunction OurBigBook.com
For n≥3 and a bounded smooth domain, a Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunction with eigenvalue λ satisfies the displayed estimate. A signed power test for a Laplacian eigenfunction and the zero-boundary Sobolev inequality give a Moser iteration with exponents pj​=2[n/(n−2)]j. The geometric series ∑j​1/pj​=n/4 gives the exact power of λ, while ∑j​(logpj​)/pj​<∞ controls the remaining constant. The constant depends only on dimension, because the zero-boundary Sobolev inequality follows by extension by zero to the whole space.
Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalue (λj​)

Dirichlet Laplacian eigenfunction OurBigBook.com
A Dirichlet Laplacian eigenvalue is a number λ for which −Δu=λu has a nonzero solution with zero boundary trace. At such a value, the shifted operator Δ+λ is not invertible.

Green’s second identity is the divergence theorem applied to phi grad psi minus psi grad phi.

Boundary term at infinity in Green's second identity (limR→∞​∫∣x∣=R​(u∂n​v−v∂n​u)dS=0)

Words: 117
Green second identity OurBigBook.com
The whole-space form of Green's second identity requires the displayed boundary limit, together with the existence of the relevant volume integrals. Pointwise decay of the fields does not by itself control their normal derivatives or the growing sphere area. In three dimensions, sufficient power bounds are u=O(r−a), ∇u=O(r−a−1), v=O(r−b) and ∇v=O(r−b−1), with a+b>1: the surface integral is then O(R1−a−b).
For a smooth counterexample to pointwise decay alone, take u=(1+r2)−1/2 and v=cosr(1+r2)−1/2. Both are smooth radial functions on all of R3 and tend to zero. Nevertheless uv′−vu′=−sinr/(1+r2), giving surface integral −4πR2sinR/(1+R2), which has no zero limit. Screened Green functions with exponential decay avoid this particular problem.

A Lie point symmetry is a continuous transformation of independent and dependent variables that maps solutions of a differential equation to solutions.

Lie point symmetry OurBigBook.com
A one-parameter point transformation has infinitesimal generator
V=∑i​ξi(x,u)∂xi​​+η(x,u)∂u​.

Its flow recovers the finite transformations.

Prolongation of a Lie point symmetry

Words: 58 Articles: 1
Lie point symmetry OurBigBook.com
The prolongation of a point-symmetry generator is its induced vector field on derivatives of the dependent variable. A generator is a symmetry of a differential equation F=0 when its required prolongation sends F to zero on the solution manifold.

ηi​=Di​η−uj​Di​ξj,ηij​=Dj​ηi​−uik​Dj​ξk.
(70)

A group-invariant solution is constant along the prolonged symmetry orbits. For a scaling of two independent variables with fixed dependent variable, it depends only on a ratio such as x/t.
